catalog_quote: Second, general observations of Kibushi suggest that there may be differences in word stress across villages and dialects. ... Stress in both Kibushi dialects is penultimate, just as in the Malagasy language (Merina dialect). But it can also fall on the antepenultimate syllable with words that end in [ka], [͡tra] and [na] [7]. ... Data from four villages were collected: Acoua and Chiconi, of Kisakalava dialect; and Ouangani and Poroani, of Kiantalautsi dialect. ... 19 of them were analyzed in order to obtain the five vowels /a, i, u, e, o/, in stressed position: ꞌhabu (long), ꞌhifi (tooth), ꞌholu(ŋu) (person), ꞌhoru(ŋu) (nose), ꞌlalaŋa (path), laꞌlahi (man), ꞌlela(ka) (tongue), ꞌliu (blood), ꞌloku (fish), ꞌluha (head), ꞌmaru (a lot), ꞌmeki (dry), ꞌnonu (breast), ꞌrohu (heart), ꞌvatu (stone), ꞌvava (mouth), ꞌviti (foot), ꞌvoru(ŋu) (bird), ꞌzahu (I) ... They reveal that stressed syllables are systematically longer than the unstressed syllables. Indeed, the median duration of stressed syllables is ... 287 ms for Ouangani (vs. 190 ms) and 270 ms for Poroani (vs. 179 ms).

new_statements.quote: There are two dialects with limited intercomprehensability: Kisakalava, used in a dozen villages with some twenty thousand speakers, and Kiantalautsi, spoken mostly in two villages, Ouangani and Poroani, by a few thousand speakers [1]. ... Second, general observations of Kibushi suggest that there may be differences in word stress across villages and dialects. ... Stress in both Kibushi dialects is penultimate, just as in the Malagasy language (Merina dialect). But it can also fall on the antepenultimate syllable with words that end in [ka], [͡tra] and [na] [7]. ... the median duration of stressed syllables is ... 287 ms for Ouangani (vs. 190 ms) and 270 ms for Poroani (vs. 179 ms).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (5 pp. All four quoted fragments are present verbatim at the stated locators: p.2 = article p.3321, left column (Introduction): 'There are two dialects with limited intercomprehensability: Kisakalava, used in a dozen villages with some twenty thousand speakers, and Kiantalautsi, spoken mostly in two villages, Ouangani and Poroani, by a few thousand speakers [1].'; right column: 'Second, general observations of Kibushi suggest that there may be differences in word stress across villages and dialects.' and 'Stress in both Kibushi dialects is penultimate, just as in the Malagasy language (Merina dialect). But it can also fall on the antepenultimate syllable with words that end in [ka], [͡…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable in both Kibushi dialects of Mayotte, including Kiantalautsi (Ouangani, Poroani); it may instead fall on the antepenult when the word ends in one of the weak syllables ka, tra, na (the pan-Malagasy pattern). The authors' own measurements on Kiantalautsi speakers show the (penult) stressed syllable is markedly longer, with an F0 rise and an intensity peak.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress 'can also' occur in words ending in [ka], [tra], [na] (stated with a citation to a Malagasy intonation study; whether all such words or a lexical subset is not said). Test words like ꞌlela(ka), ꞌholu(ŋu), ꞌvoru(ŋu) are transcribed with stress staying on the root penult when the optional final syllable is present.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly word stress ('differences in word stress across villages and dialects'); data are isolated Swadesh-list words (citation forms). The 2024 poster adds that in read declarative sentences stressed syllables remain longer and high pitch sits mostly on penultimate/ultimate syllables of the predicate.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog bush1250 'Kibosy Kiantalaotsy-Majunga' is the Kiantalautsi (Antalaotsy) variety of Malagasy spoken in Mayotte (villages Ouangani, Poroani; historically linked to the Antalaotsy of Mahajanga/Majunga), placed directly under North-Central Malagasic. The quoted source (Kassime, Hirsch & Mori 2023) studies BOTH Kibushi dialects of Mayotte and states the rule for 'both Kibushi dialects': Kiantalautsi (= bush1250; speakers recorded in Ouangani and Poroani) and Kisakalava (= Kibushi-Kimaore, kibu1236, a dialect of Antankarana Malagasy anta1255). The same paper is already the catalog source for anta1255; for bush1250 it is on-languoid because Kiantalautsi speakers were measured and named. Nothing reached describes the Madagascar-side Antalaotsy of Majunga.

new_statements.quote: L’orthographe malgache standard ne marque pas en général la place de l’accent d’intensité, qui est variable, et qui importe beaucoup pour la compréhension. Elle n’est notée traditionnellement que dans les quelques cas de mots qui seraient sans cela homographes (par exemple, en dialecte malgache de Mayotte des mots comme tanàäna « Village », différent de fanana « qu’on tient, qu’on atteint »). [...] Dans les dictionnaires, l’habitude est de marquer toujours la position de l’accent sur toutes les entrées et sous-entrées (radicaux et dérivés).
new_statements.translation: Standard Malagasy orthography does not in general mark the place of the stress (intensity) accent, which is variable and which matters a great deal for comprehension. It is traditionally written only in the few cases of words that would otherwise be homographs (for example, in the Malagasy dialect of Mayotte, words like tanàna 'village', different from tànana 'that one holds, that one reaches'). [...] In dictionaries the custom is always to mark the position of the accent on all entries and sub-entries (roots and derivatives).
new_statements.citation: Gueunier, Noel J. 2016. Dictionnaire du dialecte malgache de Mayotte (Comores). Moroni: KomEDIT / Paris: L'Harmattan, 551 pp. ISBN 9782370970237.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Kassime, Hirsch & Mori 2023: penultimate, but antepenultimate with words ending in [ka], [tra], [na]) and adds detail: Gueunier's own formulation is that the accent position is 'variable' and meaning-bearing, illustrated with exactly a -na pair (tanàna vs tànana), i.e. within the weak-final class the penult/antepenult choice is lexical and contrastive, which the 2023 rule ('can also fall on the antepenultimate') leaves open; he states no default syllable, so read alone the source says 'lexical', not 'fixed penult' (a stricter reader could log this as a type difference; I class it refines because the catalog quote itself already admits the antepenultimate…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gueunier gives no placement rule: he states that the position of the stress accent (accent d'intensité) in Malagasy, Mayotte Malagasy included, is variable from word to word and distinctive (minimal pair tanàna 'village' vs tànana 'held/reached'), that ordinary spelling does not show it, and that his dictionary therefore marks the accent on every headword and sub-entry (accented capitals, e.g. ADÀLA, HADALÀNA) and adds a bracketed phonetic transcription with a stress mark for every radical (e.g. [ta'nana]). The work is thus a per-word source of Kibushi stress positions rather than a statement of a default syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the fragments seen; one entry notes an 'accent expressif sur la première syllabe' in an emphatic pronunciation (expressive, not lexical secondary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the homograph pair tanàna / tànana (both -na final: penultimate vs antepenultimate) is cited; an etymological note contrasts Kibushi stress with Swahili kunguni [ku'guni] ('noter la place différente de l'accent'). The whole introduction was not read, so a default-penultimate sentence elsewhere in the front matter cannot be excluded (searches for pénultième, avant-dernière, tonique, accentué(e), syllabe(s), prononciation found none).
new_statements.identity_note: Gueunier 2016 describes the Malagasy dialect of Mayotte (kibushi kimaore) as a whole; whether it treats the Kiantalaotsi variety (Ouangani, Poroani) separately from Kisakalava is unknown without the front matter (Gueunier 2004 distinguishes the two). Kassime 2025, per its abstracts, covers both dialects with fieldwork in Acoua, Chiconi and Ouangani; the theses.fr EN abstract assigns Kisakalava to Chiconi and Ouangani and Kiantalautsi to Acoua, whereas the 2023 ICPhS paper (catalog source) assigns Ouangani and Poroani to Kiantalautsi and Acoua and Chiconi to Kisakalava - a point to check against the thesis when it appears.
